days.title: What Typhoons Do to Our Communities
days.objective: Learners will be able to describe at least three effects of weather disturbances (typhoons) in the Philippines.
materials: 8–12 printed pictures or large drawings of typhoon effects: flooded streets, fallen trees, damaged roofs, storm surge on a coastal road, landslide on a slope, flooded rice field (1 set per class, shown or passed around)
manila paper (1 sheet per group of 5–6 learners) and markers or crayons (1 set per group)
masking tape (1 roll) for posting group work
chalk or whiteboard marker for the Typhoon Effects web
small slips of paper for the exit ticket (1 per learner)
optional: a ball of string or yarn for the board web

flow.teacher: Greet the class and say that this week we study weather disturbances, and today we begin with what typhoons do to communities. Show the day title slide and read the 'Today' line together. Then show the question slide: 'What does a typhoon look like from your window?' Give 30 seconds of think time, then call on 3–4 learners. Accept all answers. If a learner says only 'rain', prompt: [What else happens? What about the wind or the sky?]. Build on answers in our own words. Say: [We will not tell scary stories about a specific storm; we will learn what typhoons do in general so we can describe and prepare.] Tell learners it is fine to pass if they do not want to talk about a storm.
flow.learners: Think quietly for 30 seconds, then share with a seatmate. A few volunteers answer aloud. Learners may pass if they prefer.

flow.teacher: State the goal in learner words: [By the end of today, you can name at least three effects of a typhoon on people, animals, plants, or structures.] Show the vocabulary slide and read it aloud with the class. Define typhoon again simply: a strong tropical cyclone in our part of the Pacific. Ask: [Is a typhoon only wind?] [No, it also has heavy rain.] Then show the first concept slide (strong winds and heavy rain) and connect: [Wind pushes and pulls; rain pours. Together they cause the effects we will list later.] Keep this brisk; do not lecture long.
flow.learners: Read the vocabulary aloud with the teacher. Copy the three terms and their meanings in their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the concept slide on what typhoons can cause (flooding, landslides, storm surge) using the storm-surge picture. Read the lines together. Ask: [What is a storm surge?] [Water from the sea pushed inland by the storm's winds.] Then show the second concept slide: [Why is storm surge dangerous near the coast?] [It can flood coastal houses and block roads.] If learners say storm surge is the same as a tsunami, correct gently: [A tsunami is a huge sea wave usually caused by an undersea earthquake (sometimes an undersea landslide or volcano). A storm surge is sea water pushed inland by the typhoon's winds — no earthquake needed.] Keep safety reminders: never walk or play in floodwater or near the sea during a storm.
flow.learners: Look at the storm-surge picture, listen, and answer the teacher's questions. Some volunteers explain storm surge in their own words.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide. Read the steps aloud. Say: [In your group of 5 or 6, list effects of typhoons on people, animals, plants, and structures on manila paper. You have 8 minutes. Then one reporter from each group will share.] Count off learners to form groups so it is quick; assign one group to each table or corner. While groups work, walk around and ask: [Which effect is on people? Which is on houses?] Have groups label their list with the four headings. Also add the effects of a low pressure area or monsoon rain: days of steady heavy rain and flooding even with little wind, and thunderstorms with short bursts of heavy rain, lightning and gusts. After 8 minutes, show the share-out slide. Call 3–4 groups to post or read their lists. As they share, build the Typhoon Effects web on the board in four arms: people, animals, plants, structures. Add a fifth arm for other disturbances: LPA, monsoon, thunderstorm. Ask the class to add effects not yet mentioned. Safety reminder: keep papers and bags off the floor so no one trips while moving to post.
flow.learners: In groups of 5–6, write at least three effects under each heading on manila paper. One reporter shares the group's list. The class listens and adds ideas to the board web.

flow.teacher: Point to the class web and ask: [What do we notice? Are all the effects on people?] [No, many are on animals, plants, and structures too.] Show the summary slide and read it together. Ask: [Why should we know these effects before a storm warning?] [So we can prepare: protect roofs, move to safety, store food.] Connect to this week: [Next lessons will show PAGASA's wind signals and what the weather is like before, during, and after a typhoon.]
flow.learners: Read the summary aloud with the teacher. Copy the summary in their notebooks. One or two learners answer why knowing effects helps us prepare.

flow.teacher: Say: [Now let us check what you learned today.] Show the check slide and give 30 seconds to think. Ask learners to choose silently: hands up for each option, or write the letter on a slate. Then reveal the answer and say the reason. Do NOT use the exit-ticket question here; it is different. Next, pass out slips of paper for the exit ticket: [Name one effect of a typhoon on homes.] Say learners should answer in one sentence and show a brief reason if they can. Collect the slips. If time is short, learners may answer on their notebooks instead. The exit ticket is answered on paper; the answer stays with the teacher, not on the slide.
flow.learners: Think about the check question, choose their answer silently, and watch the reveal. Then each learner writes the exit-ticket answer on a slip of paper and passes it to the teacher.

expectedObservations: Learners list more than one kind of effect, for example: roofs torn off, streets flooded, trees fallen across roads, crops flooded, animals without shelter, people losing homes.
Learners include storm surge and landslide when the pictures or web prompt them.
Learners can connect strong wind and heavy rain to the damage on structures and farms.
Some learners may focus only on homes; prompts about animals, plants, and roads should widen their answers.

check.question: Name one effect of a typhoon on homes.
check.answer: It can tear off roofs or knock down walls.
check.why: Strong winds can damage or destroy structures, and flooding can weaken foundations.

days.support: Learners who struggle to write can draw small pictures under the headings on manila paper, then say one effect aloud to a seatmate for the reporter to write. Provide a word bank on the board: flooded, fallen tree, broken roof, storm surge, landslide, muddy roads, no food. Pair a struggling learner with a confident one for the group list but require the struggling learner to say at least one effect aloud. For the exit ticket, accept a single word like 'flooded' if copied from the word bank and ask the learner to say the sentence aloud as you write the check mark.
days.extension: Early finishers can choose one effect from the class web and write two 'before the storm' actions that would reduce that effect: for example, for 'roofs torn off': ask an adult to check and tie down loose sheets while the sky is still calm; bring potted plants, toys and loose objects inside. Add the explicit rule: learners never climb roofs, cut branches, or handle wires — these are adult jobs. They can also add one effect under an extra heading, 'community services', such as power or clean water being cut.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add 5–8 minutes of group sharing: each group presents its two most important effects and explains the reason. Add a whole-class ranking task: which three effects are most common in our community, and why (near a river, near the coast, many trees). Use the extra time to let learners copy the class web neatly in notebooks as a reference for the rest of the week.

days.title: PAGASA's Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals
days.objective: Learners will be able to describe the weather conditions expected under each PAGASA wind signal (1–5).
materials: 1 chart of PAGASA Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals (signals 1–5, with wind strength, lead time, and damage descriptions) written on manila paper or shown on the TV
5 sets of index cards: each set has 5 cards with signal numbers 1–5 and 5 cards with short damage descriptions (one set per group of 5 learners)
manila paper and markers for groups that finish early (optional)
masking tape for posting the chart
a bell or clap signal for transitions

flow.teacher: Show the title slide and say: 'Yesterday we learned that typhoons bring strong winds and heavy rain that damage homes, crops, and roads.' Ask the question on the next slide: 'What do you do at home when you hear that a typhoon is coming?' Call on 3–4 learners and write their answers on the board in a simple list (e.g., buy food, charge phones, fix the roof, listen to the radio). If a learner says they climb up to fix the roof, say gently: that is an adult job for calm weather, never for children and never when the storm is near. Then show the PAGASA chart and say that PAGASA is the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, the government agency that sends wind signals so families know when and how to prepare. Tell learners that today they will learn what each signal number means. Keep this to 7 minutes; for large classes, take answers from 2 learners per row only.
flow.learners: Learners raise their hands and share what their families do before a typhoon. They listen to the teacher's introduction of PAGASA and look at the chart.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Today our goal is to describe the weather we expect under each PAGASA wind signal, from No. 1 to No. 5, and match each signal with the damage it can cause.' Show the purpose slide. Point to the chart and say: 'By the end of this lesson, you will be able to look at a signal number and say what kind of wind is coming and how long you have to prepare.' Ask: 'Why do you think a higher number means we must prepare more?' [Because the winds are stronger and can cause more damage.]
flow.learners: Learners listen to the objective and answer the purpose question orally.

flow.teacher: Show the concept slides one at a time. First: 'Higher number, stronger wind, greater danger.' Use a simple scale gesture: raise your hand higher for each signal. Second: explain lead time — 'Lead time is the number of hours before the strong winds arrive. Signal No. 1 gives about 36 hours, while Signal No. 4 gives about 12 hours, so Signal No. 4 is more urgent even though the number is higher.' Correct the misconception that signal number tells how much rain will fall: 'Signal numbers are about WIND strength, not rain. PAGASA has separate rainfall warnings.' Ask: 'If Signal No. 4 has a shorter lead time than Signal No. 1, does that mean you have more time or less time to prepare?' [Less time, so you must hurry.]
flow.learners: Learners watch the slides, copy the two key ideas in their notebooks, and answer the lead-time question.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide. Arrange the class into groups of 5–6. Say: 'Each group will get 5 number cards and 5 damage cards. Match each signal number with the damage you expect from the chart.' Hand out one set per group. Circulate and ask: 'Why did you put this damage card with this signal?' Expected answers: Signal No. 1 — very light damage, some leaves and twigs broken; Signal No. 2 — light to moderate damage, some houses made of light materials damaged, small trees uprooted; Signal No. 3 — moderate to heavy damage, many houses damaged, trees uprooted, power interrupted; Signal No. 4 — heavy to very heavy damage, many houses severely damaged, power and communication mostly cut; Signal No. 5 — extreme damage, houses destroyed, widespread power and communication cut. After matching, for each signal, have groups say/write 2-3 sentences of weather: 'Signal No. 2: the wind blows very strongly, branches and small trees bend or break, rain is heavy, walking outside is hard; Signal No. 4: violent winds, roofs blown off, rain almost horizontal.' Note that PAGASA also issues separate rainfall warnings, so heavy rain usually accompanies a cyclone even though the signal number itself measures wind. After 8 minutes, call two groups to post their matches on the board and discuss one signal at a time. Correct mistakes gently by pointing back to the chart. Remind learners there is no water or sharp object in this activity.
flow.learners: In groups of 5–6, learners lay the cards on their desks and match signal numbers with damage descriptions. They explain their reasoning to the group. Two groups post their answers on the board and the class checks against the chart.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide. Read the question aloud: 'PAGASA raises Signal No. 4. What kind of winds should you expect?' Give 30 seconds of think time, then have learners raise fingers 1–4 to vote. Say: 'Many of you chose the right answer — very strong, destructive winds within about 12 hours. The wrong choices are common: some think a higher number means more rain (it is about wind), and some think Signal No. 1 means the strongest winds (it is the mildest).' Show the reveal slide and say the correct answer and reason.
flow.learners: Learners think silently, vote with their fingers, and check their answer against the reveal.

flow.teacher: Ask: 'In your own words, why is it helpful that PAGASA numbers the wind signals from 1 to 5?' [So people can quickly know how strong the wind will be and how much time they have to prepare.] Ask: 'What should you do when you hear Signal No. 3 in your barangay?' [Prepare seriously, bring in loose objects, charge phones, follow PAGASA updates, know where to go.] Summarize: signal number = wind strength; higher number = stronger wind and more danger; lead time = hours to prepare.
flow.learners: Learners answer the questions orally and write the summary in their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Give the exit-ticket question on paper: 'PAGASA raises Signal No. 2 in your town. Describe the weather conditions you expect (wind and rain) and name one thing your family should do.' Collect the papers as learners leave. Expected answer: the wind blows strongly, branches and small trees may bend or break, rain is heavy, walking outside is hard; families should prepare, secure loose objects, charge phones, and follow updates. Do not show the exit-ticket question on the slides.
flow.learners: Each learner writes a short answer on a half-sheet of paper and submits it.

expectedObservations: Learners match most signal numbers with the correct damage descriptions, especially Signals 1, 2, and 5.
Some learners initially place the strongest damage card with Signal No. 1; they correct this after checking the chart.
Learners can state that a higher signal number means stronger wind and greater danger.
Learners can explain that signal numbers are about wind strength, not the amount of rain.

check.question: PAGASA raises Signal No. 2 in your town. Describe the weather conditions you expect (wind and rain) and name one thing your family should do.
check.answer: The wind blows strongly, branches and small trees may bend or break, rain is heavy, walking outside is hard; families should prepare, secure loose objects, charge phones, and follow updates.
check.why: Signal No. 2 warns of strong winds within about 24 hours, so families should finish their preparations today, while it is still calm.

days.support: Learners who struggle can use a simplified chart with only three columns: signal number, what the wind feels like, and one picture clue. Pair them with a stronger peer in the matching activity. If a learner answers that a higher number means more rain, gently say: 'Signal numbers describe wind; PAGASA has separate warnings for rain.' Let them point to the wind strength column on the chart and read it aloud.
days.extension: Groups that finish early can create a mini-poster showing 'What to do when Signal No. __ is raised,' choosing one signal and writing 3 actions. They can also write two sentences comparing Signal No. 1 and Signal No. 4 in terms of wind strength and lead time.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add a 5-minute role-play: one learner acts as a PAGASA announcer reading a wind signal bulletin while the class decides which preparations to make. Add a 5-minute discussion of the question: 'Why is the lead time shorter for higher signals?'

days.title: Before and During a Typhoon
days.objective: Learners will be able to sequence the weather conditions before and during a tropical cyclone, including the eye and eyewall.
materials: manila paper or cartolina, 1 per group of 5–6
markers or crayons, 1 set per group
strip cards with weather descriptions (clouds thicken, light rain starts, wind gets stronger, heavy rain and strong winds, sudden calm with clear sky, strong winds return), 1 set per group
picture set of weather scenes before and during a typhoon, 1 set per group (printed or hand-drawn if no printer)
tape or magnets for posting group work
teacher's diagram of typhoon structure (eye, eyewall, rain bands) drawn ahead on manila paper or shown as a slide image
exit-ticket slips or learners' notebooks

flow.teacher: Greet the class and remind them of last week's water cycle briefly, then point to today. Show the question slide: 'What does the sky look like before a typhoon?' Give 30 seconds of think time, then call on three or four learners. Expected answers: [dark clouds, windy, hot and humid, light rain]. Accept all reasonable observations. If a learner says 'It looks normal and sunny,' respond: 'Yes, sometimes it is still hot and calm—but the clouds and wind change soon.' Then move to the lesson purpose slide and read it aloud. Tell learners that today we will put weather scenes in order and learn why the calm middle of a typhoon is a trap.
flow.learners: Look at the question slide, think quietly, then share ideas aloud when called. Listen to the purpose.

flow.teacher: State the goal in child-friendly words: 'By the end of today, you can arrange the weather conditions before and during a typhoon, and you can explain why the calm part is not safe.' Write the word sequence on the board: BEFORE → DURING: strong wind and rain (eyewall) → brief calm (eye) → strong wind and rain again (other side of the eyewall). Ask: 'Who has ever noticed the sky turn very dark before rain?' Show the vocabulary slide with the three terms. Read each term and meaning aloud; have the class repeat 'tropical cyclone,' 'eye,' and 'eyewall' once.
flow.learners: Listen, repeat the three terms, and copy the word sequence in their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the 'Before a typhoon' concept slide and the 'During a typhoon' concept slide. Explain: before a typhoon, clouds thicken, light rain begins, and wind slowly increases—but the order can vary. During the typhoon, rain is heavy and winds are strong and gusty. Ask: 'Which happens first—light rain or strong gusty winds?' [light rain, usually, but not always]. If a learner says 'strong winds come first,' respond: 'Sometimes the wind is already strong, but usually it builds up; look at how the clouds thicken first. The important thing is to follow PAGASA signals.' Then project or post your typhoon structure diagram: the eye in the center, the eyewall ring around it, rain bands outside. Explain that the eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain. Keep this to about 10 minutes and check understanding by asking learners to point to the eyewall on the diagram.
flow.learners: Watch, listen, and answer questions. Point to parts of the diagram when asked.

flow.teacher: Group learners into 4–6 per group. Give each group a set of strip cards or picture cards of weather scenes. Say: 'Arrange these in the correct order—first what happens before the typhoon, then what happens during, then what happens if the eye passes over.' Give 5 minutes. For large classes, assign one 'card keeper' and one 'reporter' per group so materials do not get lost. Walk around and ask: 'Why did you put this after that?' Expected reasoning: [clouds thicken before rain; the calm happens only when the eye is over us; strong winds come back]. After 5 minutes, two or three groups post their sequence on the board. Compare sequences. Correct the common error that the calm means the storm is over. Safety reminder: no outdoor activity today; if anyone in the group has experienced a typhoon and feels upset, they may step aside or just listen.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, arrange the cards in order, discuss reasons, and post the sequence. Reporters explain their order to the class.

flow.teacher: Lead the class to build a summary on the board. Ask: 'What are the signs before a typhoon?' [clouds thicken, light rain, wind slowly increases]. 'What is it like during?' [heavy rain and strong gusty winds]. 'What happens when the eye passes?' [brief calm, then strong winds return from the other side of the eyewall]. 'Which part is most dangerous?' [the eyewall]. Point out the misconception: the eye is calm, but it is not the safest place—the danger returns. Show the summary slide and have learners copy the three lines.
flow.learners: Contribute answers, help build the class summary, and copy the three summary lines.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide with the multiple-choice question. Read it aloud and give 1 minute for learners to think and vote by raising fingers (1, 2, 3, or 4). Reveal the answer and briefly explain why the calm is the eye. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'During a typhoon, the rain suddenly stops and the wind becomes calm. Why should you still stay inside?' Expected answer: [You may be in the eye; the strong winds and heavy rain of the eyewall will come back soon, so it is not safe yet]. Collect the slips or check notebooks. Safety reminder: never go outside during a calm spell in a storm; wait for official announcements.
flow.learners: Vote on the check question, discuss the reveal briefly, then answer the exit-ticket question on paper.

expectedObservations: Before a typhoon: clouds thicken, light rain starts, and the wind slowly gets stronger.
During a typhoon: heavy rain and strong gusty winds continue for hours.
When the eye passes over: the sky may clear and the wind may become calm for a short time.
After the eye passes: strong winds and heavy rain return from the other side of the eyewall.
The eyewall, the ring around the eye, has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

check.question: During a typhoon, the rain suddenly stops and the wind becomes calm. Why should you still stay inside?
check.answer: You may be in the eye of the typhoon. The strong winds and heavy rain of the eyewall will come back soon, so it is not safe yet.
check.why: The eye is calm, but the eyewall around it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain, and the other side of the eyewall is still coming.

days.support: For learners who struggle, give a picture-only sequence with three cards (before → strong winds/rain → calm → strong winds again) and let them point and say one sentence for each. Say explicitly: 'the eyewall comes before the eye and again after it.' Pair them with a stronger partner and ask them to repeat the order using the words 'before,' 'calm,' and 'strong winds again.' Accept oral answers during the group report.
days.extension: Ask fast finishers to draw a labeled cross-section of a typhoon showing the eye, eyewall, and rain bands, and write one sentence explaining why the eyewall is dangerous. They can also write a 3-sentence weather broadcast script for the 'sudden calm' moment.
days.longerPeriod: If the period is 50–60 minutes, add a short demonstration: use a clear plastic cup of water, stir it in a circle with a spoon, and let learners observe the calm center while the water keeps swirling around the sides. Use only water, keep it away from electrical outlets, and wipe spills immediately to prevent slipping. Discuss how the calm center of the swirling water is like the eye of a typhoon, but with an explicit caveat: 'The water shows only that a spinning storm can have a hole in the middle. It does NOT show why: in a real typhoon the eye is calm because air sinks there, and the strongest winds are in the eyewall ring right next to the eye, not at the outer edge.'

days.title: After the Storm: Dangers and Safety
days.objective: Learners will be able to describe typical weather conditions after a tropical cyclone and identify at least one safety precaution.
materials: 4–6 printed pictures of after-typhoon scenes (flooded street, fallen tree, loose electrical wire, mud, damaged roof) — one set per group of 4–6 learners
Manila paper or cartolina, 1 sheet per group of 4–6 learners
Colored markers or crayons, 1 set per group
Masking tape for posting posters
Exit-ticket slips or 1/4 sheet of paper per learner
Chalk or whiteboard marker for the class list

flow.teacher: Show the day slide and read the title. Ask: 'What do you remember about the eye of a typhoon?' [It is calm and clear.] 'If the wind suddenly stops during a typhoon, is it safe to go outside?' [No, because the eyewall will bring strong winds again.] Then show the picture of leftover street floods and ask: 'The storm has passed and the rain has stopped. Is everything safe now?' Let 2–3 learners answer. Do not confirm answers yet; say 'Let us find out today.' For a large class, take answers from three different rows so more learners participate.
flow.learners: Recall the eye and eyewall from yesterday. Look at the picture of leftover floods. Share ideas with a seatmate, then a few answer aloud.

flow.teacher: Read the objective together: 'Today we describe the weather after a typhoon and name at least one safety precaution.' Say: 'The storm can end but the danger can stay. Today we learn what the sky and wind are like after the storm, and what is still dangerous.' Show the concept slide about weather after a cyclone, including both the weather and leftover hazards. Ask: 'After the rain stops, is the weather the same as before the storm?' [No, the sky may be clearer but floodwater remains.]
flow.learners: Read the objective in chorus. Listen and answer the teacher's question.

flow.teacher: Show the messy-after-storm slide. Explain: after a typhoon, rain and wind become weaker, but the ground is muddy, branches are on the road, and electrical wires may be on the ground. Tell them: 'Never touch a wire on the ground. It may still be live. Tell an adult right away.' Show the floodwater danger slide. Ask: 'Why is floodwater dangerous even if it looks shallow?' [It may be dirty; it can hide broken glass, open manholes, or live wires.] Show the after-weather slide: skies gradually clear or leave scattered clouds, winds become light and gusty, only occasional light rain showers, it may feel hot and humid again. But flooding and mud remain on the ground even under a calmer sky. Show the vocabulary slide and read each term: 'debris — pieces of broken things like branches and tin; live wire — a wire that still carries electricity; all-clear — an official announcement that it is safe.' Point out the wrong idea: 'Some people think the storm signal tells how much rain will fall. It tells about wind, not rain.' For a large class, use a hand signal: thumbs up if the sentence is safe, thumbs down if not.
flow.learners: Look and listen. Answer the teacher's questions. Show thumbs up or thumbs down for each safety sentence read aloud.

flow.teacher: Group the class into groups of 4–6. Give each group one picture set and one sheet of manila paper. Say: 'Make a Do's and Don'ts poster for after a typhoon. Write at least two safe actions and two dangerous actions. Use short words and a drawing.' Give 8 minutes. With many groups, assign one member as materials keeper and one as timekeeper. Walk around and ask: 'Why is this action dangerous?' [Learners explain.] Safety reminder: 'We will not use any real wires, tools, or water for this activity. We only read pictures and write. Never touch a fallen wire or wade in floodwater — this is a real safety rule, not a game.' After 8 minutes, choose 3–4 groups to post their posters and explain one rule.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, study the pictures. On manila paper, list Do's and Don'ts after a typhoon and draw simple symbols. Post the poster and explain one safety rule to the class.

flow.teacher: Show the summary slide. Ask: 'What is the weather like after a typhoon?' [Rain and wind become weaker, but floodwater and debris remain.] 'Name two dangers that can stay after the storm.' [Floodwater with hidden sharp objects or wires; downed electrical wires; open manholes.] 'When is it safe to go out?' [Only when an official announcement says it is safe.] Be sensitive: if a learner looks uncomfortable because of a typhoon experience, allow them to stay seated and not share. Correct this misconception if it appears: 'The rain stopped, so it is safe.' Say: 'No — floodwater and wires are still dangerous.'
flow.learners: Answer the review questions in chorus or by raising hands. Copy the summary lines.

flow.teacher: Give each learner a slip of paper. Read the exit-ticket question aloud twice: 'Why should you continue to stay indoors even after the rain and wind have stopped?' Remind them: 'Answer in one or two sentences. Use your own words.' Give 3 minutes. Collect the slips. If time is short, check 5 slips aloud using the answer guide. For a large class, have learners exchange and check with the sample answer you read after collecting.
flow.learners: Write their answer to the exit-ticket question on a slip of paper. Pass the slips forward.

expectedObservations: Learners identify that floodwater can hide sharp objects, open manholes, or live electrical wires.
Learners state that downed electrical wires and damaged structures are still dangerous after the rain stops.
Groups write at least two safe actions, such as staying inside until an official all-clear and avoiding flooded streets.
Some learners may say 'it is safe because the rain stopped' — this is the target misconception to correct.

check.question: Why should you continue to stay indoors even after the rain and wind have stopped?
check.answer: Because floodwater, downed electrical wires, and debris may still be dangerous; you must wait for official announcements that it is safe.
check.why: After a tropical cyclone, rain and wind are weaker, but hazards remain: floodwater can hide sharp objects or open manholes, wires may still be live, and structures may be weak. Official all-clear announcements tell people when it is safe.

days.support: For learners who struggle, pair them with a partner and give a word bank on the board: 'floodwater, wire, debris, all-clear, indoors'. Offer a sentence starter: 'It is not safe to go out because ______.' Let them draw one picture and write one safety rule instead of a full paragraph. Read the exit-ticket question aloud slowly and point to the words as you read.
days.extension: Ask early finishers to write a short announcement that a barangay official could read after a typhoon, using the phrase 'all-clear' correctly and naming two safety rules. They can also list three items a family should check at home after a storm: roof, walls, and electrical lines — with the warning to let an adult check.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, give groups 5 more minutes to finish and present their posters, with each group naming one Do and one Don't. Add a short role-play: one learner acts as a barangay official giving the all-clear announcement, and classmates ask two questions about safety. Use the extra time for 5 learners to read their exit-ticket answers aloud and receive feedback.

days.title: Typhoon Weather Challenge: Review and Assessment
days.objective: Learners will be able to review and demonstrate understanding of typhoon effects, PAGASA wind signals, and weather conditions before, during, and after a tropical cyclone.
materials: chalkboard or whiteboard and chalk/markers (1 set)
manila paper or cartolina (6 sheets, one per group)
crayons or markers (6 sets for groups)
printed pictures or drawings of typhoon effects, signal numbers, and weather scenes (1 set for the game)
index cards or small strips of paper (20 pieces) for group answers
weekly assessment sheets (1 per learner, prepared by teacher)
timer or watch (1)
tape or pins for hanging group work (1 roll)

flow.teacher: Greet the class and say: 'This week we learned about typhoons. Let's see what you remember.' Show the Day 5 title slide. Then show the question slide 'What do you remember about typhoons?' and call on 3–4 learners to share one fact each. Write their answers on the board in a simple web. Expected answers: strong winds, heavy rain, floods, signal numbers from PAGASA, the calm eye. If a learner says 'the eye is the most dangerous part,' say: 'We will check that today.' Keep the pace quick. For large classes, use a 'think-pair-share': learners turn to a partner for 30 seconds, then you call on a few pairs.
flow.learners: Learners sit in groups of 4–6. They think for 30 seconds, share one idea with a partner, then a few volunteers share with the whole class.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Today we will review typhoon effects, PAGASA wind signals, and the weather before, during, and after a typhoon. Then you will answer your weekly assessment.' Show the lesson purpose slide and read the two goals aloud. Ask: 'Why is it important to know the signal number?' Expected answers: to prepare, to know how strong the wind will be, to know when to evacuate. Say: 'Remember, the signal tells us about wind, not the amount of rain.'
flow.learners: Learners listen and read the goals. They answer the question orally.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Let's play Signal or Phase?' Show the game mechanics slide. Explain the rules: you will show a picture or read a scenario. Groups discuss for 20 seconds, then hold up a card with the correct signal number (1–5) or the correct phase (Before, During, After). Keep score on the board. Safety reminder: no running, no shouting; raise your card quietly. Use 6–8 quick rounds from the provided pictures. Example rounds: (1) A picture of a calm eye with clear sky — answer: During (eye). (2) A picture of Signal No. 3 sign and a tree bending — answer: Signal 3. (3) A picture of flooded street after the storm — answer: After. (4) A picture of dark clouds and light rain starting — answer: Before. After each round, reveal the answer. Then play one round with the multiple-choice check slide: read the question, groups choose, reveal the answer. Address the misconception: 'The eye is the most dangerous part' — correct it by showing the slide 'The eye is calm, not the worst part.' Say: 'The eyewall around the eye has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.'
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners discuss and hold up their answer cards. They listen to the correct answers and explanations.

flow.teacher: Show the summary slide with the three key ideas. Read each line aloud. Say: 'These are the big ideas to remember for your assessment.' Ask learners to read the lines with you. Quickly ask: 'What does PAGASA stand for?' Expected answer: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration. If they struggle, say it slowly and have them repeat.
flow.learners: Learners read the summary lines aloud with the teacher and repeat the meaning of PAGASA.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Now we will check what you have learned.' Distribute the weekly assessment sheets. Remind learners to write their names and to answer honestly. Read each item aloud slowly, one by one, to support learners who need help reading. Say: 'Keep your eyes on your own paper. No talking.' Monitor the class; give a 2-minute warning before time is up. Collect papers when done. For large classes, have group leaders collect the papers and place them in a tray.
flow.learners: Learners work individually and silently on the assessment. They submit their papers to the group leader.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Let's finish with our exit ticket.' Show the exit-ticket prompt slide. Read it aloud: 'What is one thing you will do differently to prepare for a typhoon because of what you learned this week?' Give learners 2 minutes to write their answer on a small strip of paper. Collect the strips. If time allows, call on 2–3 learners to share their answers. Expected sample answer: 'I will listen to PAGASA signals and prepare our house before the strong winds arrive.' Say: 'Good. Knowing the signals and the weather changes helps us stay safe.'
flow.learners: Learners write their individual answer on a strip of paper and submit it. A few volunteers share orally.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Next time we will start planning a weather broadcast script. Think about what a weather reporter says.' Show the closing slide. Quickly review the three key ideas one more time by pointing to the summary slide. Ask: 'What does the signal number tell us?' Expected answer: how strong the wind will be, not how much rain. Say: 'Remember, after the storm, floodwater and fallen wires are still dangerous. Wait for official announcements.' Dismiss the class.
flow.learners: Learners listen and answer the final question. They prepare to leave.

expectedObservations: Learners correctly match at least three typhoon effects (strong winds, heavy rain, floods, damage to homes and crops).
Learners identify that higher PAGASA signal numbers mean stronger winds and greater danger.
Learners sequence weather conditions before, during, and after a typhoon.
Learners explain that the eye is calm but the eyewall is dangerous.
Learners state at least one safety precaution after a typhoon (avoid floodwater, wait for official announcements).

check.question: What is one thing you will do differently to prepare for a typhoon because of what you learned this week?
check.answer: Sample: I will listen to PAGASA signals and prepare our house before the strong winds arrive.
check.why: Understanding signals and weather patterns helps people take safe actions early.

days.support: For learners who struggle, provide a simplified review sheet with pictures and key terms. Pair them with a buddy during the game. Read assessment items aloud and allow extra time. Use sentence starters for the exit ticket, such as 'I will ______ because ______.'
days.extension: Learners who finish early can begin drafting a 3-sentence weather broadcast script that includes a signal number and a safety reminder. They can share with their group.
days.longerPeriod: If the period is 50–60 minutes, extend the game with 2–3 more rounds, add a group sharing of exit-ticket answers, and begin planning the weather broadcast script as a class.

assessment.prompt: Which weather disturbance can flood streets and farms for days even when the wind is NOT strong?
choices: A low pressure area or habagat (monsoon) rain
A fair-weather sunny day
An earthquake
A volcanic eruption
assessment.answer: A low pressure area or habagat (monsoon) rain
assessment.explanation: LPAs and monsoon rains can pour for days and flood low places with little wind; a typhoon brings both strong wind and heavy rain.

assessment.prompt: A typhoon destroys many rice fields and coconut trees in a farming town. What is one likely result for the community?
choices: The town will have more food than before
Farmers will lose income and food may become scarce
The typhoon will make the soil better immediately
The animals and plants in the area will have more food and shelter
assessment.answer: Farmers will lose income and food may become scarce
assessment.explanation: Destroyed crops mean farmers cannot sell produce, so they lose income, and food supply decreases. Flooding and wind damage usually ruin crops and wash away soil; the area can support fewer living things afterwards, not more.

assessment.prompt: PAGASA raises Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 3. What does this tell you?
choices: There will be light rain only
Strong, dangerous winds may arrive within about 18 hours and can tear off roofs
The typhoon is already over the area
The storm is very weak
assessment.answer: Strong, dangerous winds may arrive within about 18 hours and can tear off roofs
assessment.explanation: Signal No. 3 indicates strong, dangerous winds and a lead time of about 18 hours. It is a warning about strong, dangerous winds, not just light rain. The typhoon is not over the area; the signal is issued before winds arrive. The storm is strong, not weak.

assessment.prompt: Which signal number means the strongest and most dangerous winds?
choices: Signal No. 1
Signal No. 2
Signal No. 5
Signal No. 4
assessment.explanation: PAGASA's wind signals are numbered from 1 to 5, with 5 being the strongest and most dangerous. Higher numbers mean stronger winds and greater damage potential.

assessment.prompt: During a strong typhoon, the wind suddenly becomes calm and the sky clears for a short time. What is most likely happening?
choices: The typhoon is over
The eye of the typhoon is passing over
The storm is getting stronger
It is safe to go outside
assessment.answer: The eye of the typhoon is passing over
assessment.explanation: The eye is the calm, clear center of a typhoon. When it passes over, the wind and rain stop briefly. This is not the end of the storm; the other side of the eyewall will bring strong winds again. It is not safe to go outside, and the storm is not getting stronger at that moment—it is simply the calm center.

assessment.prompt: Describe the weather after a typhoon has passed (sky, wind, rain) and name one danger that can remain even when the weather looks calm.
assessment.answer: The weather: the sky may be partly cloudy or gradually clearing, the wind light and gusty, and only occasional light rain showers; it may feel hot and humid. One danger: floodwater may remain, which can be contaminated and hide hazards like open manholes or downed power lines.
assessment.explanation: After a typhoon, the weather changes: rain and wind weaken, skies clear gradually, but flooding and debris remain. This floodwater poses risks of disease (like leptospirosis) and physical injury. The ground cannot absorb more water, and drainage systems may be blocked. Learners should recognize that the danger is not over just because the rain stopped.

assessment.prompt: Write two sentences describing the weather and one safety reminder for Signal No. 2.
assessment.answer: Signal No. 2: strong winds and heavy rain. Safety reminder: secure loose objects or stay indoors.
assessment.explanation: This short-answer item assesses learners' ability to apply wind signal knowledge and provide a correct safety reminder. It replaces the performance task so it can be completed within the timed assessment.

slides.title: Typhoons, Wind Signals, and Weather Changes
lines: Grade 5 Science · Term 3 · Week 7
Five 45-minute lessons
slides.notes: How to use this deck: each lesson starts with a "Day" slide. Speaker notes under every slide tell you what to say, what to ask and the answers to expect; they show only in Presenter View, never on the TV. Question slides come before their answer slides, so learners can think before the answer appears. The teacher guide (separate PDF) explains the science behind the week, common wrong ideas, and the full answer key.

slides.title: Day 1: What Typhoons Do
lines: Today: We describe the effects of typhoons on people, animals, plants, and structures.
slides.notes: Welcome the class. Read the today line together. Explain that this is the first lesson of a three-week topic on weather disturbances, and today is about the effects we can see and describe. Remind learners that if talking about storms feels hard, they may step out or pass. Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact. Time: about 1 minute.

slides.title: What does a typhoon look like from your window?
lines: Think for 30 seconds, then share with a seatmate.
slides.notes: Ask learners what they have seen or heard during a typhoon. Expected answers: heavy rain, strong wind, dark clouds, trees swaying, flooded streets, power out. If someone says 'a typhoon is just strong wind', respond that typhoons also bring heavy rain that causes floods. Do not collect scary personal stories; channel answers to what is seen and heard. Give 30 seconds of quiet think time, then 2 minutes of sharing. Accept answers in Filipino or English and restate in simple English.

slides.title: Words We Will Use This Week
lines: tropical cyclone — a rotating storm that forms over warm ocean water.
typhoon — a strong tropical cyclone in our part of the Pacific Ocean.
low pressure area — air pressure lower than nearby areas; often brings clouds, rain, and wind.
slides.notes: Read each term aloud and have learners repeat. Say: tropical cyclones are called typhoons here; in other places they may be called hurricanes. Clarify that low pressure area is not a storm yet; it often brings rain. Ask: [Which word means a strong tropical cyclone near the Philippines?] [typhoon]. Have learners copy the three words. Time: about 2 minutes.

slides.title: Typhoons Bring Strong Winds and Heavy Rain
lines: Winds push and pull on trees, roofs, and posts.
Heavy rain pours and can turn streets into waterways.

image.alt: A drawing of strong wind bending a tree and lifting the edge of a roof.

slides.notes: Point to the drawing. Say: strong wind is moving air; it pushes on things. Ask: [What could happen to a light roof?] [It can lift or tear.] Then say: heavy rain falls fast, and when the ground cannot take the water, the street floods. Make the link: wind and rain are the two main typhoon features we will connect to effects today. Also mention that a low pressure area or monsoon can bring days of rain and flooding without strong wind, and thunderstorms bring short bursts of heavy rain and lightning. Keep it short; the activity will do the rest.

slides.title: What Typhoons Can Cause
lines: Flooding: water covers streets, homes, and fields.
Landslides: soaked soil slides down slopes.
Storm surge: sea water is pushed onto the coast.

image.alt: A black-and-white line drawing of a coastal village being battered by a typhoon with a spiral cloud, heavy rain, strong winds bending palm trees, and a large breaking wave (storm surge) inundating hou

slides.notes: Use the drawing to define storm surge: strong winds push sea water toward the shore, and it rises above the normal level. Ask: [Is storm surge the same as a tsunami?] [No; a tsunami is a huge sea wave usually caused by an undersea earthquake (sometimes an undersea landslide or volcano). A storm surge is sea water pushed inland by the typhoon's winds — no earthquake needed.] Do not promise that storm surge happens with every typhoon. Say it can happen in coastal places. Ask if the class is near the coast or a river; connect without naming a specific storm.

slides.title: More Effects of Typhoons
lines: Homes, schools, and roads can be damaged.
Crops and trees can be destroyed.
People and animals may be harmed or lose their homes and food.
slides.notes: Use three quick questions: [Who or what can be hurt?] [People, animals, plants.] [What places can be damaged?] [Homes, schools, roads, farms.] If learners only mention homes, prompt them about farms and animals. Keep the tone factual and not frightening; say: this is why we learn to prepare. Time: about 2 minutes. Ask one learner to say one effect in a full sentence.

slides.title: List the Effects in Your Group
lines: 1. Form groups of 5 or 6 learners.
2. Draw 4 headings: people, animals, plants, structures.
3. List at least 3 effects under each heading.
4. One reporter shares your list.
Record: your group's list on manila paper.
slides.notes: Count off to make groups quickly in a large class. Give 8 minutes. Say that 'structures' means houses, schools, bridges, roads, and posts. Walk around with 2–3 prompts: [What happens to animals? What happens to crops? What happens to the road?] Remind learners to keep papers and bags off the floor so no one trips while moving. The teacher keeps this step moving: stop exactly at 8 minutes so sharing fits. Time-total for this step: 8 minutes.

slides.title: Share and Build Our Effects Web
lines: 1. Reporters come up by group.
2. Read only 2 or 3 of your best effects.
3. The class adds new ideas to the board web.
Record: the class web in your notebook.
slides.notes: Call 3–4 groups only if time is short; avoid long repetition. On the board, draw four arms: people, animals, plants, structures. Write a few words per effect, not full sentences. As reports come in, ask the class: [Is this effect on people or on structures?] If a group gives only one word like 'flooded', restate: [So the street was flooded; that belongs under structures or people?] Keep the web for use in the summary. Time: 7 minutes.

slides.title: What We Learned Today
lines: Typhoons bring strong winds and heavy rain.
These can cause floods, landslides, storm surge, and damage to homes, crops, and roads.
People and animals may be harmed or lose their homes and food.

image.alt: A drawing of a rainstorm over a small town with strong winds, bent trees, and flooding.

slides.notes: Read the summary with the class and have learners copy it. Ask: [Which effect was new to you today?] and [Why is it useful to know these effects?] Expected answers: so we can prepare, protect our homes, and know why PAGASA warns us. Tell learners that this week we will look at PAGASA's wind signals and the weather before, during, and after a typhoon. Time: about 4 minutes.

slides.title: Which is an effect of a typhoon on crops?
choices: Rice fields are flooded and plants are destroyed.
The soil turns into rock.
Plants grow taller right away.
The Sun becomes cooler.
slides.notes: Ask learners to choose silently. Give 20–30 seconds. They may show the answer with fingers (1 to 4) on the count of three so you can scan the class quickly without noise. Do not reveal until most learners have chosen. This slide prepares the exit ticket, but it is a different question. If many choose the wrong answer, revisit the concept slides about wind and rain effects. Time: about 2 minutes.

slides.title: Answer: Flooded Fields and Lost Crops
lines: Heavy rain and strong wind can flood rice fields and destroy plants.
This can also mean less food for families and animals.
slides.notes: Reveal the answer and explain the reason in one sentence. Ask: [Why are the other choices wrong?] Expected: rocks do not form from one storm; plants do not grow taller from strong wind; the Sun's heat does not change because of a typhoon. Point out that typhoon damage to crops affects the food supply, which is why farmers listen to PAGASA. Time: about 2 minutes. Then move to the exit ticket: each learner writes one effect of a typhoon on homes on a slip. Collect the slips after 3–4 minutes. The expected exit-ticket answer stays with the teacher and is not shown on a slide.

slides.title: Day 2: PAGASA Wind Signals
lines: Today: What do the PAGASA wind signal numbers mean?
slides.notes: Welcome the class and connect to yesterday: typhoons bring strong winds and heavy rain that damage homes and crops. Say today we learn about PAGASA, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration. It is the government agency that raises wind signals. Keep this short, about 2 minutes. Ask: 'Who has heard a wind signal on the radio or TV?' Take 2 or 3 quick answers to make the topic feel familiar.

slides.title: What does your family do before a typhoon?
lines: What does your family do when a typhoon is coming?
slides.notes: Ask the question and let 3 or 4 learners answer. Expected answers: buy food, charge phones, fix the roof, listen to PAGASA updates, bring in clothes. Write answers on the board in a short list. Do not judge answers; all reasonable preparations are welcome. If a learner says they climb up to fix the roof, say gently: that is an adult job for calm weather, never for children and never when the storm is near. This shows learners that families already act on warnings, which prepares them to understand why signal numbers matter. If a learner says they go outside to watch the storm, gently correct: that is dangerous. Keep to about 3 minutes.

slides.title: Our goal for today
lines: Describe the weather each PAGASA signal warns about.
Match signals 1 to 5 with wind strength and damage.
Higher number means stronger wind and greater danger.
slides.notes: Read the goal aloud in simple words: 'Today we will match each PAGASA wind signal, 1 to 5, with the wind strength and the kind of damage it brings.' Point out that higher numbers mean stronger winds and greater danger. Ask: 'Why is knowing the signal helpful for your family?' Expected: so we can prepare early and know what to expect. Keep this to 2 minutes. No need for learners to copy this slide, but they can copy the last line if time permits.

slides.title: Higher number, stronger wind
lines: PAGASA raises wind signals from No. 1 to No. 5.
Signal No. 1 has the weakest winds.
Signal No. 5 has the strongest winds and the most danger.
slides.notes: Use your hand to show a rising scale as you count from 1 to 5. Emphasize: 'Signal No. 1 is the mildest; Signal No. 5 is the strongest.' Show the full chart on the slide or poster. Explain each column: signal number, wind speed, lead time, damage, and weather. Ask: 'If the wind is already very strong, should the signal number be low or high?' [High.] Common wrong answer: learners may think Signal No. 1 means the first and therefore the strongest storm. Correct gently: 'No, the number tells the strength of the wind. Higher number, stronger wind.' Learners copy the chart or the key lines into their notebooks. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Lead time and wind signal
lines: Lead time — the number of hours before strong winds arrive.
Wind signal — PAGASA's warning based on how strong the wind will be.
Higher signal usually means less lead time to prepare.
slides.notes: Explain lead time with a simple example: 'If strong winds will arrive in 36 hours, you have more time to prepare. If they will arrive in 12 hours, you have less time.' Say: 'Signal numbers are about wind, not rain. PAGASA has separate rainfall warnings.' Ask: 'Which gives you more time to prepare — Signal No. 1 or Signal No. 4?' [Signal No. 1, because the winds arrive later.] Learners copy the two vocabulary terms. Keep to 4 minutes and check that notebooks are filled before moving on.

slides.title: Match the signal to the damage
lines: 1. Form groups of 5 to 6 learners.
2. Get 5 signal number cards and 5 damage cards.
3. Match each signal number with the damage you expect.
4. Explain your matches to your group.
5. Record your group's answers on a sheet of paper.

image.alt: Two warning sign boards side by side, one showing swirling wind lines and the other showing heavy raindrops.

slides.notes: Organize groups quickly by rows to save time. Hand out one set of index cards per group. Remind learners: this is a paper activity, no water or sharp objects are needed. Circulate and ask groups to explain one match. Expected matches: Signal 1 — very light damage, some leaves and twigs broken; Signal 2 — light to moderate damage, small trees uprooted, some light-material houses damaged; Signal 3 — moderate to heavy damage, many houses damaged, trees uprooted, power interrupted; Signal 4 — heavy to very heavy damage, many houses severely damaged, power and communication mostly cut; Signal 5 — extreme damage, houses destroyed, widespread power and communication cut. Give 8 minutes for matching and 7 minutes for sharing. If a group is stuck, point them to the wind strength column on the chart.

slides.title: Signal No. 4: what winds?
lines: PAGASA raises Signal No. 4. What kind of winds should you expect?
choices: Very light winds with almost no damage
Light to moderate winds with little damage
Very strong, destructive winds within about 12 hours
Heavy rain only, with no strong winds
slides.notes: Read the question and the four choices aloud. Give 30 seconds of think time. Then ask learners to show their answer by raising fingers 1 to 4. Do not reveal the answer yet. Watch for the common wrong choice that higher numbers mean more rain — if many choose the rain option, that is useful to discuss after the reveal. Count how many chose each option silently to yourself but do not announce the tally yet. Keep this to 2 minutes.

slides.title: Answer: very strong winds
lines: Signal No. 4 means very strong, destructive winds.
They may arrive in about 12 hours.
The signal is about wind strength, not rain amount.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct choice. Say: 'Signal No. 4 means very strong, destructive winds that may arrive within about 12 hours and can heavily damage many houses.' Point back to the chart. Address the common wrong answer: 'Some of us chose the rain option. Remember, the signal number is about wind. PAGASA gives separate warnings for heavy rain.' Ask: 'What should your family do if Signal No. 4 is raised in your town?' [Prepare immediately, secure the house, follow updates.] Keep this to 3 minutes.

slides.title: What we learned today
lines: PAGASA raises wind signals 1 to 5.
Higher number means stronger wind and greater danger.
Each signal gives a lead time so people can prepare.
Signal numbers are about wind, not rain.
slides.notes: Read the summary aloud and have learners copy it into their notebooks. Ask one or two learners to restate the summary in their own words. Remind them that the exit ticket will ask about Signal No. 2, so they should think about what strong winds can do. Keep this to 3 minutes. If time is short, learners may copy only the first two lines.

slides.title: Day 3: Before and During a Typhoon
lines: Today: We will put weather scenes in order.
We will learn why the calm part of a typhoon is not safe.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and read the day title aloud. Point to the two lines: today is about the order of weather before and during a typhoon, and about a calm part that tricks people. Say: 'By the end, you will be able to explain why we stay inside even when the rain stops.' Keep this to about 1 minute. Do not mention the eye yet; that comes later so learners can discover it. If a learner has experienced a typhoon, keep the tone calm and say we will talk about safety, not scary stories.

slides.title: What does the sky look like before a typhoon?
lines: Think for 30 seconds, then share with a seatmate.
slides.notes: Ask learners to think for 30 seconds, then call on three or four. Expected answers: dark clouds, the wind picks up, it feels hot and humid, light rain may start. Do not correct a learner who says 'sunny,' because before a typhoon it can still be hot and clear; say: 'Yes, it can still look normal, but soon the clouds thicken and the wind changes.' This question is just to activate their own experience, so accept all reasonable observations. Note which learners mention clouds and wind, because you will connect this to the lesson later. This slide is a plain question, not a multiple-choice test.

slides.title: Our goal for today
lines: Arrange weather scenes from before to during a typhoon.
Explain why the calm part is not safe yet.
slides.notes: Read the goal aloud in child-friendly words. Tell learners they will work in groups to put weather cards in order, and then learn about the calm center of a typhoon. Write on the board: BEFORE → DURING. Say: 'We will also learn a word for the calm center.' Keep this to about 2 minutes so there is time for the group activity. Ask one learner to repeat the goal back to the class.

slides.title: Words we will use today
lines: tropical cyclone — a big rotating storm over warm ocean water, called a typhoon here.
eye — the calm, clear center of a typhoon.
eyewall — the ring around the eye with the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
slides.notes: Read each term and meaning aloud. Have the whole class repeat 'tropical cyclone,' 'eye,' and 'eyewall' once. Say: 'In the Philippines, we usually call a strong tropical cyclone a typhoon.' Explain: 'The eye is a small clear circle in the middle of a much larger storm; the eyewall is the narrow ring of towering clouds hugging the eye, and that ring is where the winds are strongest.' Ask: 'Which word means a calm center?' [eye]. 'Which word means the ring of strong wind and rain?' [eyewall]. If a learner says the eye is the most dangerous part, say: 'We will check that idea in a few minutes.' Keep to about 3 minutes.

slides.title: Before the typhoon
lines: Usually the clouds get thicker and darker.
Wind and rain build up — but the order can change.
Sometimes it still looks calm while the storm is near. Follow PAGASA signals.
slides.notes: Explain the typical order: usually the clouds thicken first, then light rain starts, and the wind slowly increases; but this is not a strict rule. Sometimes strong gusts and heavy squalls arrive before any steady rain, and sometimes the sky still looks clear and sunny while the storm is near. That is why we follow PAGASA signals, not just what we see out of the window. Ask: 'Which comes first, light rain or strong gusty winds?' [Usually light rain first, but not always — squally gusts can come first.] Emphasize the word 'slowly'—this is the time families use to prepare. Connect to the wind signal lessons from Day 2: this is the lead time. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: During the typhoon
lines: Rain is very heavy and winds are strong and gusty.
It can last for hours. Stay inside and stay dry.

image.alt: A thunderstorm with heavy rain, strong wind bending trees, and dark clouds

slides.notes: Explain that during a typhoon the rain is heavy and the winds are strong and gusty, and this can last for hours. Say: 'Gusty means the wind comes in strong blasts.' Ask: 'Is it safe to play outside during this time?' [no]. Safety reminder: never go outside during heavy rain and strong wind. Keep this short, about 4 minutes, because the next slide explains the eye and eyewall. Do not describe violent details; keep the tone calm and focused on safety.

slides.title: The eye and the eyewall
lines: The eye is the calm, clear center with little wind or rain.
The eyewall is the ring around it with the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

image.alt: A circular ring of storm clouds with lightning bolts and rain falling downward, surrounding an empty central space.

slides.notes: Post or show the typhoon diagram. Point to the center: that is the eye, which is calm and clear. Point to the ring around it: that is the eyewall, where the strongest winds and heaviest rain are. Ask learners to point to the eyewall on the diagram. Ask: 'Which part has the strongest winds?' [eyewall]. If a learner says the eye is most dangerous because it is the center, say: 'That is a good guess, but we will see in the next activity why the calm eye can trick people.' About 5 minutes; this is the key idea for today.

slides.title: Put the weather scenes in order
lines: In your group, look at each weather card.
Arrange all 6 cards: before, strong wind and rain, the short calm if the eye passes, then strong winds again.
Explain your order to the class.
Record: draw your order in your notebook.
slides.notes: Give each group a set of weather cards or strips. Model the first step: 'Before—clouds thicken and light rain starts.' Set a 5-minute timer. For a large class, assign a card keeper and a reporter per group so materials stay together. Walk around and ask 'Why did you put this after that?' Expected reasoning: clouds thicken before rain; the calm happens only when the eye passes over; strong winds return after the calm. A sequence is only correct if strong winds and heavy rain appear both before and after the calm card. After 5 minutes, two or three groups post their sequence. Watch for groups that put 'calm' at the end—that is the misconception to correct. Safety note: if a learner becomes upset, let them step aside and just listen.

slides.title: What to remember
lines: Before: clouds thicken, light rain starts, wind slowly gets stronger.
During: heavy rain and strong gusty winds.
If the eye passes: it gets calm, and then strong winds return. Stay inside.
slides.notes: Build this summary together on the board first, asking learners for each line, then show the slide. Ask: 'Which part is most dangerous?' [the eyewall]. 'Is the calm eye a safe time to go out?' [no, because the strong winds return]. Have learners copy the three lines into their notebooks. Tell them not to memorize numbers of signals here—that was Day 2. Keep to about 5 minutes. Check that notebooks have all three lines before moving on.

slides.title: The rain stops and it feels calm. What now?
lines: The rain stops and the sky clears during a typhoon. What should you do?
choices: Go outside to check the damage.
Stay inside because strong winds may return.
Play outside while it is calm.
Open all the windows and doors.
slides.notes: Read the question aloud. Give 1 minute for learners to think, then have them vote by raising fingers (1, 2, 3, or 4). Do not reveal yet; ask two learners to explain their choice. This check tests whether they apply the eye/eyewall idea. Keep the pace calm. Note that this is different from the exit-ticket question that comes after, which asks learners to explain in their own words. About 2 minutes before the reveal.

slides.title: Why we stay inside
lines: Correct answer: Stay inside because strong winds may return.
The calm may be the eye. The eyewall winds come back soon.
slides.notes: Reveal the answer and explain: the calm may mean the eye is passing over, and the eyewall on the other side will bring strong winds again soon. Ask: 'Who chose option 1 or 3? What will you do next time?' Let one or two learners respond. Safety reminder: after a calm spell, never go outside until adults and PAGASA say it is safe. Then hand out exit-ticket slips and ask the exit-ticket question on paper; collect or check notebooks. About 8 minutes for the reveal plus exit ticket.

slides.title: Day 4: After the Storm
lines: Today: What is still dangerous after a typhoon?
slides.notes: Greet the class and read the title. Say in plain words: 'The strong wind and rain are only part of a typhoon. Today we look at what happens after.' Ask: 'What did we learn yesterday about the eye of a typhoon?' Expect: it is calm and clear. Ask if the calm eye means the danger is over; expect 'no'. Tell them today's lesson teaches how to stay safe after the storm. Timing: 2 minutes for this slide. Be mindful that some learners may have experienced a typhoon; keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact, not scary.

slides.title: Is it safe after the rain stops?
lines: The rain and wind have stopped.
Is it safe to go outside now?

image.alt: A simple drawing of floodwater standing in streets and fields under a calmer sky.

slides.notes: Show the picture of leftover street floods. Ask: 'What do you see?' [Water still on the street, a calmer sky.] Ask: 'Is everything safe now?' Let two or three learners answer but do not confirm yet. Expect some to say 'yes, the rain stopped' — that is the common wrong idea we will correct today. Say: 'Keep your idea. We will check it after we learn.' Timing: 3 minutes. Do not tell learners the answer on this slide; the correct idea comes later. Safety note: we are only talking about floodwater, not going near it.

slides.title: Weather after a tropical cyclone
lines: Sky clears slowly or stays partly cloudy.
Wind becomes light and gusty; only light showers.
It may feel hot and humid again.
Floodwater and mud stay even under a calmer sky.
slides.notes: Explain gently: after a tropical cyclone, the rain and wind lessen, but that does not mean everything is fixed. The sky may clear gradually, and it may feel hot and humid, but floodwater may stay for days, roads may be blocked, and buildings may be weak. Ask: 'Why is a house with a damaged roof still dangerous?' [It may fall or leak; it is not stable.] Remind learners that we follow official announcements from the barangay or the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, or PAGASA, and from the local government. Timing: 3 minutes. Avoid giving any specific numbers about how long floods last; just say 'may stay for a while'.

slides.title: Dangers left by the storm
lines: Branches and tin may block the road.
Electrical wires may be on the ground.
Never touch a wire. Tell an adult.

image.alt: A simple drawing of a muddy yard with a fallen tree branch and a broken electrical wire on the ground.

slides.notes: Point to the fallen branch and the wire in the drawing. Say: 'Debris means pieces of broken things, like branches, tin, and glass. They can cut you or block the road.' For the wire, be firm but calm: 'A live wire is a wire that still carries electricity. Never touch it, even with a stick or slippers. Tell an adult right away.' Ask: 'What will you do if you see a wire on the ground?' [Do not touch it; tell an adult.] Timing: 4 minutes. This is a real safety rule; repeat it once more before the activity.

slides.title: Why floodwater is dangerous
lines: It may be dirty and cause sickness.
It can hide sharp objects and open manholes.
It can hide live wires.
slides.notes: Explain that floodwater is not clean water. It can carry dirt and germs from canals and garbage, so wading in it can make people sick. It can also hide broken glass, open manholes, and wires. Ask: 'Why should you not play in floodwater?' [It is dirty; it can hide sharp things; it can be deep.] Correct the idea 'shallow water is always safe' by reminding them that even shallow water can hide danger. Timing: 4 minutes. Do not give statistics; keep it general.

slides.title: Words for today
lines: debris — pieces of broken things, like branches and tin
live wire — a wire that still carries electricity
all-clear — an official message that it is safe
slides.notes: Read each word and its meaning aloud. Have the class repeat. Ask: 'Give one example of debris you saw after a storm.' [A branch on the road, broken glass, pieces of tin.] Explain that an all-clear is not a guess by a neighbor; it comes from officials. Make sure learners understand that 'live' here does not mean alive like a person; it means it still carries electricity. Timing: 3 minutes. Write the three words on the board so learners can use them in their posters.

slides.title: Make a safety poster
lines: 1. Study your picture with your group.
2. Write two Do's and two Don'ts.
3. Draw one simple safety sign.
4. Post your poster on the wall.
Record: two safe actions and two dangers.
slides.notes: Before starting, remind everyone: 'No real wires, tools, or water in this activity. We only read pictures and write.' Put learners in groups of four to six and give each group one picture set, one manila paper, and markers. Set a time limit of 8 minutes and count down at the last two minutes. Walk around and ask groups to explain their rules. Common mistake: writing 'go outside to play when the rain stops' — respond by asking what could be on the road. Choose three or four groups to present after posting. Timing: 15 minutes including presentations. Watch for learners who look upset; let them work quietly without presenting.

slides.title: Remember after the storm
lines: Rain and wind get weaker, but danger stays.
Floodwater and wires can still hurt you.
Go out only after an official all-clear.
slides.notes: Read the summary aloud and let learners copy it. Ask two or three quick questions: 'Name one danger that stays after the rain stops.' [Floodwater, wires, debris.] 'Who tells us it is safe?' [Officials and PAGASA, through an all-clear.] If a learner says 'the rain stopped so it is safe', gently correct: 'The rain is only one part; floodwater and wires can still be dangerous.' Timing: 4 minutes. Keep the statement that the eye is calm but the danger is not over, connecting to yesterday.

slides.title: Show what you know
lines: Answer on your paper in one or two sentences.
slides.notes: This is the exit ticket. Read the question aloud twice: 'Why should you continue to stay indoors even after the rain and wind have stopped?' Give learners three minutes to write on their slips. Expected good answer: because floodwater may hide sharp objects or wires, wires may still be live, and officials have not yet said it is safe. If a learner writes 'because the rain stopped', that is incomplete; mark it as needing follow-up. Collect all slips. Timing: 8 minutes including collection. Do not write the answer on the slide; it stays in your notes for checking.

slides.title: Day 5: Typhoon Weather Challenge
lines: Today: We will review typhoons, signals, and weather changes.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and set a positive tone. Say: 'This week we learned about typhoons. Today we will review and then you will answer your weekly assessment.' Remind learners that it is okay to feel nervous about tests, but they have learned a lot. Keep this slide up for about 1 minute. For large classes, have group leaders help distribute materials later.

slides.title: What do you remember about typhoons?
lines: Think for 30 seconds. Share with a partner. Then share with the class.
slides.notes: Ask learners to think-pair-share. After 30 seconds, call on 3–4 volunteers. Expect answers like: strong winds, heavy rain, floods, signal numbers from PAGASA, the calm eye. Write their answers on the board in a web. If a learner says 'the eye is the most dangerous part,' respond: 'We will check that today.' Do not correct yet; save it for the game. This activates prior knowledge from Days 1–4.

slides.title: Our goals for today
lines: Review typhoon effects, PAGASA signals, and weather before, during, and after a typhoon.
Show what you know on the weekly assessment.
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud. Emphasize that the assessment is a chance to show what they have learned, not to be afraid of. Ask: 'Why is it important to know the signal number?' Expected: to prepare, to know how strong the wind will be, to know when to evacuate. Remind them that PAGASA stands for Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration. Keep this slide for about 2 minutes.

slides.title: Signal or Phase?
lines: 1. Look at the picture or listen to the scenario.
2. Talk with your group for 20 seconds.
3. Hold up your card: a signal number (1–5) or a phase (Before, During, After).
4. Keep score.
slides.notes: Explain the rules clearly. Show that groups have cards with signal numbers 1–5 and phase words. Say: 'No shouting, just raise your card.' Safety reminder: no running. Play 6–8 rounds using the provided pictures. Example rounds: calm eye with clear sky (During), Signal No. 3 sign and tree bending (Signal 3), flooded street after storm (After), dark clouds and light rain starting (Before). Reveal answers after each round. Keep score on the board to motivate.

slides.title: Which part of a typhoon is the most dangerous?
choices: The eye, because it is the center
The eyewall, because it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain
The outer clouds, because they are the biggest
The calm part, because it tricks people
slides.notes: Read the question and options aloud. Give groups 20 seconds to discuss and hold up their answer choice. Do not reveal yet. This checks the common misconception that the eye is the most dangerous. If groups choose 'the eye,' that is expected; address it in the next slide. Keep the pace quick, about 2 minutes.

slides.title: The eyewall is the most dangerous part
lines: The eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
The eye is calm, but the danger is not over.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct answer: the eyewall. Explain: 'The eye is calm, but it is surrounded by the eyewall, which has the strongest winds and heaviest rain. When the eye passes over, the wind stops for a short time, but then the other side of the eyewall brings strong winds again.' Ask: 'Why is it dangerous to go outside during the calm?' Expected: because the strong winds will come back soon. Connect to Day 3.

slides.title: The eye is calm, not the worst part
lines: The eye is the clear center of a typhoon.
The eyewall around it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
Never go outside during the calm of the eye.

image.alt: A top view of a typhoon showing a calm, clear circular center called the eye surrounded by swirling clouds.

slides.notes: Reinforce the difference between the eye and the eyewall. Say: 'The eye looks peaceful, but it is a trap. The other side of the storm is coming.' Ask: 'What should you do if the wind suddenly stops during a typhoon?' Expected: stay indoors and wait for official announcements. Emphasize safety: this is not to scare them but to keep them safe. This slide is a concept reinforcement after the reveal.

slides.title: Remember these big ideas
lines: Typhoons bring strong winds, heavy rain, floods, and damage.
PAGASA signals 1–5 warn about wind strength and lead time.
The eye is calm, but the eyewall is dangerous. After the storm, floodwater and debris are still risky.
slides.notes: Read each line aloud and have learners repeat after you. These are the key ideas they need for the assessment. Ask: 'What does PAGASA stand for?' Expected: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration. If they struggle, say it slowly and have them repeat. Keep this slide for about 2 minutes. Tell learners to keep these ideas in mind as they answer the assessment.

slides.title: Weekly assessment time
lines: 1. Write your name on your paper.
2. Read each item carefully.
3. Answer on your own. No talking.
4. Submit your paper to your group leader when done.
slides.notes: Distribute the assessment sheets. Remind learners to write their names. Say: 'Keep your eyes on your own paper. No talking.' Read each item aloud slowly for learners who need help reading. Monitor the class and give a 2-minute warning. For large classes, have group leaders collect papers and place them in a tray. Collect all papers before the exit ticket. Allow about 13 minutes.

slides.title: What will you do differently to prepare?
lines: Write one thing you will do to prepare for a typhoon.
Use this sentence: I will ______ because ______.
slides.notes: This is the exit ticket. Give learners 2 minutes to write their answer on a strip of paper. Collect the strips. If time allows, call on 2–3 volunteers to share. Expected sample answer: 'I will listen to PAGASA signals and prepare our house before the strong winds arrive.' Accept any reasonable answer that shows understanding of preparation. This assesses their application of the week's learning. Keep it positive and encouraging.

slides.title: Next time: weather broadcast planning
lines: Next week we will plan a weather broadcast script.
Think about what a weather reporter says and shows.
slides.notes: Close the lesson by previewing next week's performance task. Say: 'Next time we will start planning a weather broadcast script. Think about what a weather reporter says.' Quickly review the three key ideas by pointing to the summary slide from earlier. Ask: 'What does the signal number tell us?' Expected: how strong the wind will be, not how much rain. Remind them: 'After the storm, floodwater and fallen wires are still dangerous. Wait for official announcements.' Dismiss the class.
